bottleneck: Seizure prediction would transform epilepsy care, but pre-ictal brain states are inconsistent across patients and even across seizures in one patient. Intracranial recordings show warning signatures minutes ahead in some cases and none in others, and false alarms erode trust in any warning system until patients ignore it. The dynamical transition into seizure — the bifurcation the brain undergoes — is not understood well enough to forecast reliably, and non-invasive signals are too coarse to capture it.
current_state: Responsive neurostimulation reacts to seizure onset rather than predicting it. True forecasting remains a research goal with false-positive rates too high for clinical use.

title: Epileptic seizures resist reliable prediction
why_it_blocks: Without prediction, therapy is always reactive — intervening after the seizure has begun. Forecasting would enable prevention instead of damage control, restoring independence to millions who live in fear of the next event.
